title: Fast synthesis of high surface area bio-based porous carbons for organic pollutant removal
author: Wu, Zhang, et al.
materials: Unburned surface boreal peats, including feather moss and sphagnum peats, were cored in PVC columns (H = 15 cm) from the Pelican Mountain Research Site (55°36’ N, 113°35’ W), Alberta, Canada. These two species were chosen as precursors because they are the most dominant moss species in the boreal spruce peatlands. Large twigs, plant roots and wood debris were manually removed. Sphagnum peat sampling and processing steps are shown in Fig. 1 as an example. Live feather moss was easily separated from underlying decomposed peats. Sphagnum, however, had no clear boundary with the underlying decomposed peat. Hence, the entire 15 cm sphagnum peat soils were picked as the feedstock. Feather moss and sphagnum samples were dried at 105 °C overnight in an oven to constant weight, ground and sieved (Fisher, dia. 8 inch) to less than 2 mm size. Post-burn peats were simulated through heating feather moss and sphagnum samples in a muffle furnace (Fisher Scientific, USA) at 300 °C for 30 min. 300°C was selected because this was within reasonable range of temperatures that peat fires occur (i.e., 250–300 °C) [10]. Moreover, we picked corn starch (Sigma-Aldrich) and cellulose (Sigma-Aldrich) as precursors, due to their low cost and abundance in North America, as well as their potential to partly mimic peat constituents, i.e., polysaccharidic and lignocellulosic substances. Corn starch and cellulose were also oven-dried at 105°C overnight to constant weight. Preliminary experiments indicated that raw starch swelled significantly upon heat treatment and formed tar products with very low surface area after chemical activation. However, a previous study obtained high surface area spherical carbons through KOH activation from heat-stabilized cassava starch [11]. Here a similar approach was taken, where corn starch was first stabilized in a muffle furnace at 220 °C for 16 h to eliminate starch chain hydroxyl groups and melt the crystallites. The stabilized starch was further pulverized by a coffee grinder, then passed through a 2 mm sieve. Cellulose was not further treated prior to the activation. The biomass feedstocks, including unburned feather moss, unburned sphagnum, 300 °C lab-burned feather moss, 300 °C lab-burned sphagnum, 220 °C heat-stabilized corn starch and cellulose, were respectively labelled as Fm, Sph, BFm-300, BSh-300, BCS-220 and CL.Fig. 1A schematic presentation of main processing steps for obtaining sphagnum derived porous carbons.Fig 1

Fm, Sph, BFm-300, BSph-300, BCS-220 and CL were respectively impregnated with ZnCl2 (anhydrous, ≥97%, Sigma-Aldrich) at a mass ratio of 1:3. All impregnated samples were well-stirred by a glass rod before chemical activation. Certain masses of these mixtures were loaded onto a quartz boat (100 × 15 × 75 mm), which was then transferred into a quartz tube. Before the pyrolysis, the tube furnace (Thermocraft Inc., USA) was preset to 200 °C. Samples were heated up to 400 °C at a rate of 7 °C/min and maintained for 1 h, or 600 °C at a rate of 13 °C/min and maintained for 1 h, under constant nitrogen flow (100 mL/min). After the reaction, the 400 °C treated samples were directly removed from the chamber, whereas the 600 °C treated samples were allowed cooling in the chamber for 20 min under N2 flow before removing. The products were washed with 30 mL 1.0 M HCl (Sigma-Aldrich) followed by 1 L DI water until constant effluent pH, followed by drying overnight at 105 °C in an oven. The obtained porous carbons were respectively labelled as FmZC-T, SphZC-T, BFmZC-T, BSphZC-T, BCSZC-T and CLZC-T, where T (°C) refers to the activation temperature. The detailed physicochemical characterizations of the as-prepared biomass porous carbons were described in our previous publication [8].

steps.title: Collect and preprocess biomass
steps.instruction: Core unburned surface boreal peats (feather moss and sphagnum) in 15 cm PVC columns, manually remove twigs, roots and wood debris, dry samples at 105 °C overnight to constant weight, grind and sieve to ≤2 mm size.

steps.title: Simulate post‑burn peat
steps.instruction: Heat dried feather moss and sphagnum samples in a muffle furnace at 300 °C for 30 min to mimic peat fire conditions (250–300 °C).

steps.title: Stabilize corn starch
steps.instruction: Dry corn starch at 105 °C overnight to constant weight, then heat‑stabilize in a muffle furnace at 220 °C for 16 h, pulverize with a coffee grinder and sieve through a 2 mm mesh.

steps.title: Impregnate feedstocks with ZnCl₂
steps.instruction: For each feedstock (Fm, Sph, BFm‑300, BSph‑300, BCS‑220, CL) add anhydrous ZnCl₂ (≥97 %, Sigma‑Aldrich) at a mass ratio of 1 : 3, stir thoroughly with a glass rod until uniformly mixed.

steps.title: Load samples into furnace
steps.instruction: Place measured amounts of the ZnCl₂‑impregnated mixtures onto a quartz boat (100 × 15 × 75 mm), insert the boat into a quartz tube, and set the tube furnace (Thermocraft Inc., USA) to 200 °C before starting the pyrolysis program.

steps.title: Pyrolyze and activate carbon
steps.instruction: Under a constant nitrogen flow of 100 mL min⁻¹, heat the samples:

substeps.instruction: Ramp to 400 °C at 7 °C min⁻¹, hold for 1 h, then remove the boat directly from the chamber.
Ramp to 600 °C at 13 °C min⁻¹, hold for 1 h, keep the chamber under N₂ for an additional 20 min cooling before removal.

steps.title: Wash and dry activated carbons
steps.instruction: Wash each carbon product with 30 mL of 1.0 M HCl (Sigma‑Aldrich), then rinse with 1 L de‑ionized water until the effluent pH is constant, and dry overnight at 105 °C in an oven. Label the products as FmZC‑T, SphZC‑T, BFmZC‑T, BSphZC‑T, BCSZC‑T or CLZC‑T, where T is the activation temperature (400 or 600 °C).

steps.title: Prepare phosphate buffer (pH 7, 20 mM)
steps.instruction: Dissolve 1.165 g NaH₂PO₄·H₂O and 3.097 g Na₂HPO₄·7H₂O in 1 L de‑ionized water, verify pH ≈ 7 (20 mM). Use this buffer for all adsorption experiments to keep pH constant (variation < 0.3).

steps.title: Establish UV‑vis calibration curve
steps.instruction: Prepare a series of p‑nitrophenol standards in the phosphate buffer, measure absorbance with a DU800 UV‑vis spectrophotometer (Beckman Coulter, USA) at the maximum wavelength of 400 nm, and generate a calibration curve for concentration determination.

steps.title: Perform adsorption isotherm tests
steps.instruction: For each desired p‑nitrophenol concentration (20–2000 mg L⁻¹):

substeps.instruction: Transfer 25 mL of the buffered solution into a 50 mL conical flask.
Add 10 mg of the prepared porous carbon sorbent.
Stir at 200 rpm on a multiposition stir plate at 20 °C for 24 h to reach equilibrium.
Filter the suspension through a 25 µm PVDF membrane.
Dilute the filtrate as needed (e.g., 4×, 20×, 50×, 100×) and measure absorbance at 400 nm using the calibrated UV‑vis spectrophotometer.

steps.title: Conduct adsorption kinetics experiments
steps.instruction: Using a 20 mg L⁻¹ buffered p‑nitrophenol solution:

substeps.instruction: Place 25 mL of the solution in a flask and add 10 mg of sorbent.
Stir at 200 rpm on a multiposition stir plate at 20 °C for the desired contact time (0–4 h).
At each time point, withdraw the suspension, filter through a 0.2 µm PVDF membrane, and measure the filtrate absorbance at 400 nm.
